This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo’s toxic chemical spill, SCOTUS to review a home distilling case, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Diageo’s toxic spill contaminates “pristine” Scottish river: The water in Scotland’s River Spey was once some of the cleanest in the world until a chemical spill from Diageo’s Cardhu Distillery. Contamination from the incident killed thousands of salmon, trout, and other fish. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) is actively investigating Diageo to see how the caustic soda, the toxic contaminant, entered the waters. A Diageo spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company is complying with SEPA and helping plan regeneration and restoration measures.
  • Supreme Court agrees to hear ban on home distilling case: Supreme Court decided on Monday to hear the case that will determine if the 1868 federal ban on home distilling is unconstitutional. The justices reached the decision following a request for review from Trump’s Department of Justice, which it filed after the SCOTUS had put a delay on deciding whether or not to hear the case. Hearings will begin as early as January.
  • Fawn Weaver motions to block Uncle Nearest sale: As three potential buyers eye Uncle Nearest its assets, founder Fawn Weaver filed a motion to stop the sale. The filing came after Uncle Nearest’s court-appointed receiver Phillip G. Young, Jr., said in a court document on Oct. 9 that the whiskey brand neared sale under Chapter 11.
  • Beloved bev-alc trade show slims after attendance drops: Bar Convent Berlin (BCB), one of the beverage industry’s most influential trade events, will shrink from three days to two days of festivities in 2027 as this year’s attendance dropped by 1,000 visitors and over 100 exhibitors year-over-year. The event’s organizer RX Deutschland said BCB’s trimming-down is part of a broader strategy that will prioritize other in-person trade events of other sizes.

Product releases to watch:

  • Absolut Vodka partners with Charli xcx for product drops, merch: Absolut announced a two-year partnership with the hyperpop icon who made waves with her 2024 album “brat.” The collab will entail limited-edition product drops, branded glassware, and fan activations.
  • Jay-Z and LVMH’s Champagne brand launches a vertical-tasting bundle: Armand de Brignac — also known as Ace of Spades — founded by Jay-Z and now co-owned by LVMH, released a vertical tasting pack for two of its Blanc de Noirs expressions. The pack, priced on its website for $2,500, includes both the Blanc de Noirs Assemblage No. 4 and No. 5 and is limited to just 100 cases.

content:
In the Mile High City, the fight is on for the future of the middle tier.

A brewer threw the first punch — or at least, the first one in the public eye. In early September, Constellation Brands, the country’s third-largest macrobrewer, told its wholesaler in Denver, Coors Distributing Company (CDC), that it was terminating its arrangement within 30 days. Mark Anthony Group, which ranks fourth behind the Modelo maker in off-premise sales, followed suit less than two weeks later. Sierra Nevada Brewing Company, the country’s second-largest craft brewer by Brewers Association-defined production volume, made its own move for the exit earlier this month.

The dominoes fell so fast, and from a westward territory, that your humble Hop Take columnist heard echoes of Republic National Distributing Company’s collapse in California, which started with rapid-fire departures by major liquor suppliers at the top of 2025, and ended with the mega-distributor’s de facto demise earlier this year. Was it a social contagion? Blood in the water? Something else?

It’s in vogue for beverage-alcohol industry c-suiters to blame abstractions like “headwinds,” and “Zoomers” whenever trouble arises. But my reporting on RNDC’s California cataclysm indicated bad business decisions, institutional arrogance, and infrastructural rot had pushed the firm to the brink right as the hangover in post-Covid booze sales began to bite. There are always causes, and some are always more proximate than others.

So what’s the casus belli for Colorado’s middle-tier trench war? The militants aren’t saying much.

“We’re exploring all legal and commercial options,” CDC tells Hop Take via email. “None of the parties provided any reason for their termination and doing so without cause is a direct violation of the Colorado beer franchise law.” The firm, a wholly owned distributorship of Molson Coors Brewing Beverage Co., has already asked Denver’s district court to enjoin Constellation and Mark Anthony from exiting; it is “evaluat[ing] next steps with Sierra Nevada.”

“We have concluded our partnership with Coors Distributing Company and remain grateful for their partnership over the years,” says Ellie Preslar, Sierra Nevada’s chief growth officer, in an emailed statement. “Though this was a difficult decision, it is necessary for both the long-term and short-term needs of our business.”

A spokesperson for Constellation declined to comment, citing the litigation. Mark Anthony did not respond.

What gives? I doubt it’s frustration over facilities. After all, in a bit of incredibly unfortunate timing, CDC just cut the ribbon on a new state-of-the-art, 70,000 square-foot warehouse at the end of August, less than two weeks before Constellation’s pink slip. If you work at or with CDC, and know more, please get in touch by emailing dave@dinfontay.com or texting dinfontay.11 on Signal. (You can remain anonymous in my coverage.) But in the meantime, tune your ear to another echo of RNDC’s retreat from the Golden State, because suppliers aren’t just leaving CDC — they’re heading to Reyes Beverage Group. Or at least, trying to.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but often rhymes, and it’s rhyming in the Rockies right now. “How much RNDC blood is on Reyes’s hands in California?” I asked in a column the week I broke the news that the now-defunct distributor was exiting the market last year. “Maybe more than you think.” I was never able to verify whether RBG was in talks to acquire RNDC CA before its exit, as some sources had claimed. But there’s no doubt the mighty beer-turned-”total beverage” distributor’s fierce, many-fronted competition in California hastened RNDC’s failure there. Most of the suppliers who fled pre-collapse, fled to RBG.

A few states east and 18 months later, Mark Anthony and Sierra Nevada have signaled their aims to move their CDC volume to RBG. Constellation has been playing coy, but it’s almost unfathomable that it would move to another house. In a remarkable turn of industry fate, RBG acquired its Colorado operation just this year from, you guessed it: RNDC. Its entry into the state, along with Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits’ acquisition of Eagle Rock Distributing Co. earlier this year, has shifted the middle-tier calculus there. Now, CDC is facing subtraction.

(Laurel Slick, RBG’s vice-president of corporate affairs, provided statements to Hop Take welcoming Mark Anthony and Sierra Nevada to the fold.)

But. But! While CDC execs may be uttering f-words privately, they’re uttering another f-word publicly: franchise. The history of franchise law is long, winding, and deathly boring, but the upshot is that beer distributors are nearly unique in the protections afforded to them by most states’ laws. The most crucial of these is the so-called “just cause” provision, which requires brewers to cite a legally defensible breach of their agreement with the house they’re trying to terminate. This provision is written into most states’ codes because wholesalers marched on statehouses to make it so in the ‘60s, ‘70s, and ‘80s. Critics argue it harms competition by making it difficult for good brewers to bail on bad distributors; boosters insist it protects competition by making it difficult for bad brewers to strong-arm good distributors. But it’s there.

The protective power of this provision was tested most famously in Florida roughly a quarter-century ago, and distributors came away with the whip hand. In Maris Distributing v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc., a wholesaler fought the brewer tooth and nail for a decade over a termination it believed unjust. The family — the kin of baseball great Roger Maris, who’d been bestowed an A-B house by Gussie Busch after finishing out his Hall of Fame career with the St. Louis Cardinals — won a $120 million settlement in 2005.

As the mantra goes: there are 50 different states, and 50 different three-tier systems. A version of the just-cause clause is on the books in Colorado. But it’s a weird version. It dictates a brewer hoping to terminate a distributor has to cite “alleged noncompliance” and allow the offending firm 60 days to “cure” the infraction. If the distributor doesn’t shape up in that time, then the brewer can ship out. That’s all right at the top of C.R.S. § 44-3-408. But in subsection three, the code appears to contradict itself, noting “the supplier shall have the right to terminate an agreement with a wholesaler at any time by giving the wholesaler at least ninety days’ written notice by certified mail.” To me, a not-lawyer, , the Colorado code appears to say that a brewer must have just cause to terminate a distributor after 60 days, but can terminate for any reason after 90 days.

You will not be shocked to learn that this is not how CDC’s actual lawyers read the text. “Under Constellation’s novel interpretation of Colorado law, its termination will become final after 90 days,” the firm’s legal team wrote in a September 25 filing. “In the interim, there is a likelihood that CDC will face cascading terminations from its other suppliers.”

For a trade that has long grasped the power of a united political bloc, CDC’s existential fight is cause for alarm. At the National Beer Wholesalers Association’s (NBWA) annual conference in Orlando in mid-October, president and chief executive Craig Purser sounded the klaxons. “The efforts to weaken the three-tier system are going to keep coming, and that’s why we need you to double down on your support and participation in NBWA and your state’s association,” he said, per a dispatch from Brewbound.

Whether the suppliers’ assessments of Colorado’s code are innovative, or illegal, is a matter for the judicial system. But in the meantime, if you’re wondering who the hell would write a statute like that, well, the independent beverage-alcohol bar (ahem) is too. Colorado’s franchise law is “really badly written,” Drew Jaglom of Tannenbaum Helpern Syracuse & Hirschtritt LLP told a presumably sympathetic crowd at the NBWA confab, Brewbound reported.

“What good is a statutory right to cure a breach if a supplier can bypass it simply by waiting another thirty days?” asks Ashley Brandt, the Tucker Ellis LLP attorney behind the prolific trade blotter Libation Law Blog, in a post about the CDC brew-haha. “A supplier that cannot establish a breach—or knows the distributor will fix it—could simply choose the ninety-day route. What happens during those additional thirty days that makes a performing distributor’s continued contractual compliance irrelevant?”

It’s a good question. For CDC, it may wind up being the question. And with the pendulum of power lately swinging back towards big suppliers, you can bet the rest of the middle tier will be hanging on the answer.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Well, Halloween is right around the corner, so it’s a good thing your costume is already covered. What’s that? You’re not wearing the Adult Wedgehead Jumpsuit Costume ($69.99)? The totally epic apparel that corresponds to Shock Top’s Candy Corn Wheat Ale, a new and not-at-all-depressing collaboration between Tilray Brands and retail Grim Reaper Spirit Halloween? Huh. I mean… why not?

📈 Ups…

Stone Brewing co-founders Greg Koch and Steve Wagner are taking over the firm’s recently closed World Bistro & Gardens in Escondido… First-wave craft-brewing pioneer Deschutes will take a crack at the booming “hard sports drink” space with a malt-based offering, Firelyte… Sapporo USA says it has a path to double last year’s volume by the end of 2027… The absolute rubes who bought Ultra Right 100% Woke-Free American Beer back in 2023 still haven’t received it, and Georgia’s attorney general is now investigating, lol… Twin Cities icon Summit Brewing found a new lender to take over its about-to-be-foreclosed-upon loans…

📉 …and downs

Pioneering craft-brewing supplier Admiral Malting announced plans to shutter… Mega-brewers Constellation Brands and Mark Anthony Group are jumping into the “hard sports drink” segment, too — with vodka-based offerings… Centi-billionaire and known freak (but I repeat myself) Mark Zuckerberg finally figured out how to make Guinness look uncool…

content:
Oysters are a glamorous dish. Often served on a lofty tower over a pile of crushed ice, they gleam and glisten as they await a spritz of lemon juice or dash of mignonette. Pair the bivalves with some Champagne, a salty Sancerre, a crisp Martini, or even a pint of Guinness, and you’re in for a glitzy treat.

What’s less glamorous, however, is actually ordering oysters. Whether at a dedicated raw bar with an in-depth oyster menu or a casual restaurant with just a few varieties listed, names like “Blue Point,” “Pemaquid,” and “Bombazine” can seem like a foreign language. And unlike wine lists, which are typically accompanied by a sommelier to guide guests through complex terms, having an oyster expert on deck is a bit less common.

Snapping an Instagrammable pic of the aesthetically arranged half shells is one thing — but getting the exact flavor and texture that you want is another. Depending on the variety and location of origin, oysters bring a wide range of flavors. Before diving into the menu, it can be helpful to decide whether you want creamy, almost sweet oysters or briny ones that taste like a gulp of fresh salt water. Beyond flavor, you should also determine if your preferred texture is meaty and hefty or lean and easy to swallow.

To help make your oyster-ordering experience a bit easier, VinePair tapped Ben Crispin, general manager at Maison Premiere, one of Brooklyn’s most celebrated raw bars, to describe the flavors and textures of 15 different varieties. With his help, we charted the oysters across two scales: briny to creamy and lean to meaty.

Next time you find yourself face-to-face with a menu of unknown oyster varieties, turn to this guide to make sure you know what you’re getting.

content:
Working in the service industry, one of the biggest parts of the job is to meet the expectations and wishes of guests. In restaurants, hosts and servers are the business’ first point of contact with the patrons. They are tasked with making sure specific needs are met, such as flagging any allergens or grabbing extra utensils. Likewise, chefs also frequently bend to the whims of their customers, whether that be cooking a burger to a certain temperature or removing raw onions from a side salad.

Most customer modifications are welcome and reasonable, and are a normal part of working in kitchens. But occasionally, a request will come through the kitchen that’s just outright bizarre. That’s why we asked 10 chefs from around the country to name the weirdest demands they’ve ever seen on an order ticket.

From marshmallow fluff dolloped onto a steak to a “vegan” egg white omelet, these are the craziest dish modifications that guests have asked for, according to chefs.

The weirdest dish mods chefs have ever received:

  • Marshmallow fluff on everything
  • Deep-fried steaks
  • Prime rib sandwich mixed into farmhouse salad
  • Ground ribeye burger served with packaging labels
  • No ginger, garlic, onion, or cilantro
  • Steak cooked half-rare and half-well done
  • Well-done steak tartare
  • Non-fried fried oyster mushroom sandwich
  • Vegan egg white omelet
  • Well-done tuna tartare
  • Caesar salad without the lettuce
  • Exactly seven French fries
  • Hamburger that isn’t on the menu

“Early on, a family brought their own marshmallow fluff and asked us to put it on everything their kids ate, including the steak, fries, and salad. We did it, and it was the most disgusting thing I’ve ever seen. We’ve also had guests ask us to cook their steak in the deep fryer because they only eat things that are deep-fried.” —Mark Bucher, co-owner, Medium Rare, New York City

“A few months after opening Millstone, we had a guest request one of the more unusual modifications I’ve seen: combining our smoked prime rib sandwich with our farmhouse salad. They wanted everything — the warm, thinly-shaved smoked ribeye, caramelized onions, melted provolone, mixed field greens, seasonal vegetables, and crumbled goat cheese — all chopped up and tossed together with our horseradish aioli as the dressing. Essentially, they turned two completely different dishes into one very unconventional steak salad. Nearly a year into service, it’s still one of the most memorable requests we’ve received.” —Tyler Murray, chef, Millstone, Lexington, Ky.

“One of the strangest modification requests I’ve had was a guest who asked us to grind a ribeye steak to make his burger, replace the fries with a salad, and bring out the original packaging for every ingredient so he could personally verify the allergens. He told us he had both a citrus allergy and a ‘greens allergy,’ and said that the price should be reduced because he wasn’t getting the standard sides. After about 40 minutes of us trying every possible way to accommodate him, he took off his shoes and socks and put them on the empty chair next to him. When we finally explained that there were simply some requests we couldn’t safely or reasonably fulfill, he responded, ‘So the chef is refusing to make my meal?’” —Clinton Snowling, vice president of culinary operations, Parched Hospitality Group, NYC and West Palm Beach, Fla.

“Cilantro, ginger, garlic, and onion are part of every Indian and South Asian dish, especially on Drāvida’s menu. One of the craziest modifications was when a guest walked in and said they cannot eat ginger, garlic, onion, nor cilantro. We still made it happen: We made them two amazing dishes from scratch using spices and herbs that would make the sauces flavorful. Instead of using onions, we used leeks and they enjoyed it.” —Aarthi Sampath, chef and founder, Drāvida, NYC

“I have worked in a variety of styles of kitchens, so I’ve seen some weird stuff. But I think the modification that takes the cake was when someone asked for a flat iron steak cooked half-rare and half-well done. Then, the server came back to the kitchen and said the guest was adamant about it ‘not being cut in half,’ which I still think about it to this day. Thankfully, the guest was eventually receptive to ordering another dish.” —Mikey Miller, chef, Field Note at The Ashbrook Hotel, Frankfort, Ky.

“One of the strangest requests I’ve ever received was for a well-done steak tartare. Considering the dish is traditionally served raw, it definitely caught me and our team off guard. At that point, you’re not really ordering steak tartare anymore, but we did our best to capture the flavors of the dish.” —Adam Plitt, executive chef, Delmonico’s Hospitality Group, NYC

“The weirdest dish modification I’ve ever gotten was when a guest didn’t want anything fried, but still wanted a fried oyster mushroom sandwich. So, I had to roast all the ingredients in the oven. It took significantly longer to make, like upwards 30 minutes for a sandwich that otherwise took less than three minutes to get out. The server that was helping the table tried to direct them to items on the menu that didn’t include any fried elements, but they were set on this particular item and then lectured me on the unhealthiness of frying food. Nonetheless, it was very early in my career, and I didn’t know it would have been much easier to say, ‘No.’” —Haley Duren, executive chef, Long Count, NYC

“We were asked to cook a shared ribeye half-medium rare and half-well done because the couple liked different temperatures. We’ve also gotten ‘medium rare, but closer to rare’ and, my personal favorite, ‘medium rare, but cooked through with no pink.’ Someone also once asked for an egg white omelet with no yolk or cheese because they were vegan. We’ve also had requests for an omelet with no eggs, just mushrooms and spinach.” —Barry Tonks, culinary director, IGC Hospitality, NYC and Orlando, Fla.

“One of the most unusual requests I’ve received was for a tuna tartare, but well done. It caught me off guard because raw tuna is what defines the dish. Of course, every guest has their preferences, but that request has certainly stayed with me. The second of the strangest requests I’ve received was for a Caesar salad without the lettuce, just the croutons, parmesan, and dressing. It turned into more of a Caesar salad-inspired snack, but in a restaurant, part of the fun is figuring out how to make a guest’s request work.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef, Merchants Hospitality, NYC and Nashville

“Two unusual requests stand out to me. I had one customer who would always order French fries, but insist on exactly seven pieces, no more and no less. Another guest would regularly order hamburgers for the entire table, even though they weren’t on the menu at the seafood restaurant where I worked. He would leave an enormous tip and keep coming back.” —Teddy Kim, culinary director, Oiji Mi and bōm, NYC

title: Federal Judge Dismisses Suit Against Costco Over 100% Agave Claims
summary:

The consumer rights firm Hagens Berman filed the case with the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington at Seattle in November last year after amassing 14 plaintiffs to join the class suit.

content:
On Friday, a federal judge dismissed a class action lawsuit against Costco and its private label Kirkland Signature that alleged the “100% de agave” claims on its tequila bottles were fraudulent and misleading. The consumer rights firm Hagens Berman filed the case with the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington at Seattle in November last year after amassing 14 plaintiffs to join the class suit.

The suit claimed Costco knowingly sold tequila with “significant presence of non-agave sugars,” despite labeling its products — including Kirkland Blanco Tequila, Reposado Tequila, Añejo Tequila, Añejo Cristalino Tequila and Extra Tequila Añejo — as “100% de agave” and as “100% agave azul.” The plaintiffs cited results from Site-Specific Natural Isotope Fractionation-Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (SNIF-NMR) testing, a method commonly used by government bodies and other regulatory agencies to compliance-check food and beverage products.

The plaintiffs asserted that Costco’s claims misled consumers, and that they would have steered away from Kirkland’s tequila or paid significantly less had they known it was not made entirely of pure agave. The case also alleged Costco knowingly acquired a false “100% de agave” certification that allowed it to sell its tequilas, which range from $18.69 to $48.99, at high prices in the U.S.

The warehouse grocery chain defended its labels by citing product tests conducted in Mexico, which turned out different results than the plaintiffs’ SNIF-NMR. It also pointed to former cases with similar allegations against, in which a U.S. judge ruled the SNIF-NMR as insufficient evidence to debunk the “100% de agave” label.

Costco is not the only tequila vendor to be thrown under question for its pure agave claims. Last month, a New York judge tossed a similar case against Diageo’s Casamigos and Don Julio brands over insufficient testing. Allegations against Kendall Jenner’s 818 Tequila’s “100% agave” labels have also led to a class action lawsuit, which the company has motioned to dismiss multiple times to no avail.

content:
Increasingly, a bottle of wine these days seems to arrive with an artist attached; on a label, via a vineyard commission, through social media scrolls. The rationale for these arty collaborations is by now well-rehearsed: to attract new audiences, differentiate a brand, and increase cultural capital.

“Art enables us to connect with a cultured audience, and is also a good way to keep your brand alive,” says Fabien Vallérian, the international director of arts and culture at Ruinart, which has ostensibly been at it since 1896, when Alphonse Mucha, an Art Nouveau artist, designed the first ad for the Maison. Against shifting drinking habits and crowded shelf space, linking wine to art can signal higher value, create buzz, and lend innovation credentials to a brand.

The question is whether it works for the everyday wine brands themselves, whether it serves smaller scale producers running on tight margins, and whether audiences who pay for art and cultural access in other contexts value wine the same way.

The empirical basis is thin. Research into arts sponsorship finds plenty of potential for goodwill and engagement (who doesn’t like the thrill of opening the post-launch party goodie bag in the cab home?), but less evidence of what happens at the till. Consumer studies can show an “art infusion” effect, in which visual art can raise perceived value and luxury associations, while eye-tracking studies of wine labels have found pictorial elements attract the most attention, and label attractiveness predicts willingness to pay. But the effect varies by artwork, product, and consumer, and brands themselves rarely publish controlled sales data capable of proving a return.

Impecunious arts organizations expect product donations from wine brands, which suggests a shaky grasp of the latter’s balance sheet. Wine is capital-intensive business with tight, often impossible margins, few brands can afford to bankroll another “collab” and hope some cultural capital sticks, so it’s worth separating the various forms the wine-art relationship takes in the market today, and asking what each is actually for.

The Prestige Exception: When the Bottle Becomes the Object

The art-plus-wine model has been propelled by blue-chip Champagne brands over the past three decades, where the boundary between wine and art object blurs. Since the 2006 vintage, Louis Roederer has collaborated with French designer Philippe Starck on its zero-dosage Brut Nature, a project Starck accepted only once he could have input into the cuvée itself. Dom Pérignon‘s collaborations with world-renowned and commercially successful artists include Jeff Koons’ 2013 Balloon Venus, built around Rose Vintage 2003; labels for Vintage 2015 using Jean-Michel Basquiat’s “In Italian” (Basquiat died in 1988); and Takashi Murakami’s designs for Vintage 2015 and the first Rosé Vintage 2010. Veuve Clicquot handed the design of La Grande Dame 2012 to Yayoi Kusama.

Such limited editions, launches, and their relaunches keep these brands in conversation and turn the wine and especially its packaging into sought-after objects for collectors more than drinkers — Kusama’s numbered sculpture 71/100, complete with a bottle of La Grande Dame 2012, sold at auction for £87,720 in January. But prestige editions reveal little about whether art sells ordinary wine in ordinary quantities.

Back in the still wine aisles, rarely does a season pass without a wine “doing art,” partnering at a gallery launch, or doing a restaurant activation tie-in. There are charitable one-offs, a separate economy from selling wine: in 2013 a nine-litre Salmanazar of Ornellaia 2010, customized by Michelangelo Pistoletto, sold for £80,000 at Sotheby’s, then the highest price paid at auction for a single bottle of Italian wine.

“The wine was first and the fact of doing things differently than things had been done before was first. And then art came to partner on this adventure.”

At the everyday end, Campo Viejo has put street artists including Okuda San Miguel and Remed on supermarket-priced Riojas, with Pernod Ricard citing distinctive packaging among drivers of growth to a record three million cases annually by 2020; Prophecy Wines built its core range around Victo Ngai’s tarot-like illustrations; while Ecco Domani, Santero, and even Aldi have used artist or designer labels to distinguish their bottles.

The Label: What It Can and Cannot Do

The artist label is the most established form of partnership. It is most convincing when a genuine bond joins winery and artist, a shared philosophy legible in both bottle and image. Without it, the strategy reads as a marketing ploy rather than a statement and loses both audiences at once. Its lineage traces to Château Mouton Rothschild, where in 1924 Baron Philippe commissioned Jean Carlu, a graphic designer, to reinterpret the family crest for his first vintage label. The gesture celebrated the mise en bouteille au château milestone, as much as aesthetics, a signal of radical innovation in the industry, like an avant-garde manifesto.

“The wine was first and the fact of doing things differently than things had been done before was first. And then art came to partner on this adventure,” says Julien de Beaumarchais de Rothschild, co-owner of Château Mouton Rothschild, who oversees the estate’s relationship with artists. The labels have become a roll-call of the most commercially significant 20th-century artists since Braque created the label for the 1955 vintage. Dalí followed in 1958, Picasso’s estate for the 1973 release (posthumously to mark promotion to first growth), Warhol designed 1975 vintage label; canonical now, but each in their own time matched the estate’s spirit of disruption and innovation.

Here is the inconvenient finding. Across 52 post-reveal reviews covering the past 12 vintages of Chateau Mouton’s grand vin, only seven named the artist, two described the artwork and none incorporated it into the wine’s score or qualitative judgement. This might suggest the trade and wine nerds treat the artist as paratext, just promotional material outside the serious evaluation of the wine. That approach misses what an Olafur Eliasson (2019) or an Anish Kapoor (2009) is signalling on a Mouton artist label: a form of translation, giving voice to a year or a region, making visible the most immaterial things a wine can hold: transmitting terroir.

This is why the label works hardest when producer and artist share a cause. In 2009, South Africa’s revered winemaker, Eben Sadie, made six wines from old vines, released as a series of 280 boxed sets, with ink-wash drawings and collages inspired by their West Coast vineyards drawn by its most important artist, William Kentridge, a known oenophile. “It wasn’t about business — at no point money was exchanged,” Sadie says. “It was about putting something out there to say, here’s part of our history in wine,” a history in wine and art that had been once overlooked by both wine and art markets.

At the other end sit intimate stories, almost inside jokes between wineries and artists captured on a label design. Leeuwin Estate’s Art Series has featured Australian artists since its first vintage in 1980, with each label carrying its own anecdote — from a better deal on a John Kelly than the National Gallery managed, to keeping all four of John Olsen’s frog drawings for its Riesling, to co-founder Tricia Horgan continuing to scout artists for the collection (“I’ve got my eye on you,” she tells them). Gut Oggau’s bottles each carry the face of an invented family member drawn by Jung von Matt, ageing a little with every vintage. Cult wines such as Montevertine’s Le Pergole Torte continue to feature vintage labels illustrated with the elegant mystery women drawn by Alberto Manfredi, even after his passing.

The Estate As Gallery

A different kind of partnership forms through oenotourism, with sculpture parks and gallery spaces drawing visitors to the other side of the bottle. Italy is exemplary: around 60 wine-producing sites exist, according to the University of Verona. These are heirs to a tradition of placing contemporary art in rural spaces that runs back to the 1960s. The Ceretto estate in Piedmont reports its Sol LeWitt and David Tremlett designed Barolo Chapel draws at least 30,000 visitors a year, and at least another 10,000 visiting the winery. From Ca’ del Bosco, to Castello di Ama, to Feudi di San Gregorio, to Vini Planeta, tastings unfold among commissions and collections.

Here, art plausibly does sell wine through the captive audience and experiential pleasure of drinking wine where it is made. But the more compelling examples involve skin in the game: owners committing personal capital, land, and years to cultural projects that become part of the foundation rather than an annual marketing line. Places like Bodega Colomé where Donald Hess planted a museum devoted to James Turrell 2,300 metres up in the Andes. Or David Walsh blasting and burrowing his subterranean Museum of Old and New Art (MONA) three levels into the sandstone beneath Moorilla’s historic Pinot Noir vineyard on Hobart’s Berriedale Peninsula in Tasmania. The commercial logic of bringing people physically onto a wine estate is clearer more generally. Wine Australia found 66.7 percent of cellar-door visitors bought wine during their visit, averaging 4.42 bottles, while follow-up research found a 16 percent net gain in buyers among those who’d never previously bought a brand.

“We believe artists are the best ambassadors to raise awareness about ecology. You’re not just there to drink Champagne, you’re also there to think about protecting the planet.”

Château La Coste in Provence is an exemplary case: since it opened in 2011, art has been continuously integrated into the landscape, with sculptures and pavilions by Tadao Ando, Frank Gehry, and Tracey Emin making the domain a cultural destination in its own right. Official tourism figures recorded 200,000 visitors in 2017, rising to a reported 400,000 annually in 2024. The estate’s development director, Jérôme Scheher, says 25 percent of its 700,000 bottles are sold directly onsite.

Owner Paddy McKillen’s friendships with the architects and artists make the results organic. In June, the estate released Madame ‘B’, a rosé from the 2025 vintage, in an inaugural run of 10,000 bottles carrying a butterfly design by Damien Hirst continuing a long-standing friendship between the pair and of Hirst’s 2024 estate-wide exhibition, “The Light That Shines.” “The château is a place we both love and from which we draw inspiration,” McKillen says. The continuing build-out, including a wine school and more cellar space, puts the cultural project into the winery’s long-term development rather than an annual activation budget.

You Are Cordially Invited: The Art x Wine Event

Commissions and sponsorship can tie a wine to a cultural moment, borrowing audiences and associations that conventional advertising struggles to reach. England’s burgeoning wine industry is a revealing case. In its 2025 Industry Report, WineGB has sales up 200 percent between 2018 and 2024, reaching 9.1 million bottles, while producers have become increasingly culturally acquisitive. Artelium Wine Estate commissions artists across labels and exhibitions; Balfour Winery commissioned artists to interpret its limited Winemakers’ Collection; Nyetimber is taking the Ruinart route, attaching English sparkling wine to sponsorship of cultural institutions from the National Gallery to the V&A and Design Museum. Vines take years to mature; cultural capital can be acquired rather faster. Getting the art world to drink your wine for free is one thing; getting it to pay for the next bottle is another.

Since 2018 the historic Veronese producer Pasqua has invested nearly €6 million in contemporary art encompassing labels, immersive installations, exhibitions, and programs. CEO Riccardo Pasqua says the aim is to reach consumers through “entertainment, beauty, and lifestyle”, opening the winery to spaces once considered “unorthodox.” Its ‘Artistic Projects’ open call this year drew over 200 applications, and selected Sara Ricciardi whose installation appeared at Palazzo Maffei during Vinitaly. Here, the investment is substantial and sustained; the puzzle is still measurement. Exposure, attendance, and engagement can be counted, isolating the arts’s effect on sales is harder. A delighted opening-night audience delighted at the opening is not yet a customer at the till.

The buzz generated by continuous events can also hide the better work. Ruinart excels at presence at the fairs and biennales, the art world guzzling its blanc de blancs, but the glamor obscures a serious arts commissioning program running since 2008, asking artists such as Vik Muniz and David Shrigley to answer questions on climate change, sustainability, and nature, now extended to a younger roster of commissioned artists and designers. “We believe artists are the best ambassadors to raise awareness about ecology,” says Frédéric Dufour, president of Maison Ruinart. As if on cue, the American artist Andrea Bowers, a participant in this Conversations with Nature commission, adds: “You’re not just there to drink Champagne, you’re also there to think about protecting the planet.”

The Verdict: Attention Is Not a Sale

It is a crowded moment for collaborations between almost everything and the art world, and a brand that places an artwork on a bottle and calls the result “art” enters an increasingly skeptical field. The evidence suggests that art can influence how consumers see wine: attracting attention, raising perceived value, making a bottle memorable, and in the right setting, encouraging purchase or visit. What remains harder to prove is whether the artwork itself produces sustained incremental sales rather than a temporary lift in attention or footfall.

That makes the nature of the partnership matter. The strongest partnerships require patience, capital, and commitment beyond an annual campaign; the credible ones feel almost accidental, incidental to what the winery was doing anyway. Mouton’s labels grew from commitment to innovation; La Coste’s commissions from friendship and sustained project pipeline; Ruinart’s core arts engagement from years of investment in a theme. Independent producers, struggling with the usual pressures at the best of times, rarely have that luxury.

As collaborations multiply, consumers have also become more practiced at reading them. Once the museum or gallery moves onto the small space of a label, into an event or across an estate, the artwork and cultural claim are judged alongside the wine. Art can change what a consumer notices and remembers. Whether it changes what they buy depends on more than putting an artist’s name on the bottle.

Though Zinfandel’s rich history reaches back to the vineyards of Croatia, the grape variety has had a massive impact on wine drinking culture in the U.S. Originally brought to California by a Boston ship captain, the Zinfandel grape carried winemakers through the Gold Rush and through the evolution of California wine country. Though Cabernet Sauvignon took over as the variety dominating the conversation around California wine, there are still some producers who embrace Zinfandel as one of the state’s most important grapes.

Because of this history, California boasts a number of hidden pockets of old vine plantings that date back 50 to over 100 years. The wines made from these sites often have the term “old vines” on the label to indicate the grapes were sourced from one of these longstanding plots. On this list, you’ll see families that have been farming this grape for generations, long before Cab was king.

From bottles that showcase Zinfandel’s bold, ripe fruit character to those that feature a more restrained side — plus a few from its original home in Croatia — here are the 30 best Zinfandels to drink in 2026.

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.

Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff samples thousands of bottles every year. This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and — importantly — price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

VinePair’s tasting panel evaluates every wine on its aromas, flavors, structure, balance, and quality. We also consider whether or not the wine showed typicity for its specific grape or region.

How We Compiled This List

In order to provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Zinfandels to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

For the Zinfandel roundup, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based on the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria of best Zinfandels to buy right now. Each wine was assessed on quality, price, and availability to compile the final list.

The Best Value Zinfandel

Cline Family Cellars Ancient Vines Zinfandel 2024

This wine comes from a disappearing AVA. Contra Costa Valley is there, but the threat of urban development is real because of its proximity to the San Francisco Bay. For wine historians and preservationists, this land is part of America’s deep wine history. Most of the vines here are 100 to 140 years old, first planted in the mid-19th century. Bottles are on the market right now from vineyards that no longer exist.

Families like the Clines, among others, are trying to keep this vineyard land alive with bottles like the Ancient Vines Zinfandel. It captures the history of how we became a wine-drinking culture and is a worthy purchase to help preserve our viticultural history. The Zin grapes are sourced from a vineyard located on the sandy banks of the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, with some vines reaching well over 100 years old. The result is a wonderfully concentrated wine, with impressively rich character for its under-$25 price point. It has a savory nose with blackberry and tea notes. It also has a hint of aged balsamic and vanilla bean. The palate is delicious and juicy, with soft fruit supported by medium acidity. This is a wine you should buy a lot of and have on hand to impress your friends with awesome American wine.

The Best Splurge Zinfandel

Matthiasson Old Vine Zinfandel 2022

Last year we dubbed the Gagnon-Kennedy Monte Rosso Zinfandel as the most splurge-worthy. It made this list again this year, and it was a joy to experience the vintage variation. It is still a big, beautiful, powerful Zin. So this year we’re spotlighting a wine of the same caliber, but a completely different style.

Steve and Jill Matthiasson started Matthiasson Wines in Napa in 2003 with the goal of working with sustainable farming practices to make balanced, refined wines in a region more known for its bold, high-ABV wines. And with this Zinfandel, they show a wonderfully light, focused example of the variety.

Grapes for this bottling were sourced from Sonoma’s Armor Plate Vineyard, a dry farmed, organic vineyard that was planted in the 1890s. It is a stunning example of Zinfandel, with crushed wild berries and cured black olives flecked with a light dusting of peppercorns. The palate is a study in balance and restraint, with a soft, elegant mouthfeel that still pronounces its personality, medium fruit depth, and almost perfect acidity. This wine is in complete harmony.

The Best Zinfandels Under $30

Tortoise Creek Organic Zinfandel 2023

In a rush and need a solid red wine for dinner? This is your bottle. At this price, the variety on the label is often lost to large-scale production. But Zinfandel thankfully refuses to be pushed to the back, with its character coming through loud and clear in this 100 percent varietal wine. It’s easy drinking and balanced. While not the most complex, it gives everything you might want from a casual weeknight wine, with plush fruit, soft tannins, and good acidity.

Phil Coturri was farming organically and biodynamically before it was cool, or at least since 1979. The Sixteen 600 winery is a Coturri family project started in 2007 to continue this amazing legacy, making small-batch, single-vineyard wines from organic sites across Sonoma. This wine blends Zinfandel with a splash of Grenache and Petite Sirah, creating a rich, juicy wine with pops of freshness. There’s clove, cracked black pepper, wild berry jam, and a touch of cinnamon on the nose. It has a soft, rich mouthfeel with an easy tannic frame, letting the fruit and acidity shine.

This bottling comes from the Dalmatia region, produced by a family that has been tending these vines since the 15th century. It is peppered with plum and blackberry jam aromas on the nose, with a waft of earth. The palate is wonderful, with a rustic edge tamed by beautiful, expressive fruit. FAQs

Where is Zinfandel from?

Originally, the Zinfandel grape was from the country of Croatia. DNA profiling in the late ‘90s shows that it has the same genetic makeup of the native Tribidrag grape, also known as Crljenak Kaštelanski.

Where is Zinfandel grown?

Zinfandel as we know it grows mostly on the West Coast of the United States. It is mostly concentrated in the Dry Creek AVA and the Lodi AVA, though it is prevalent across Sonoma County. It can also be found in smaller quantities in Oregon and Washington State.

What is old-vine Zinfandel?

There is no official definition for old-vine Zinfandel but it is generally agreed upon that a vine 50 years or older is considered “old” or “ancient.” Some consider 30 years to be enough. Since there are so many historic sites in California, it’s more common to see this designation on Zinfandel bottlings from the state than other grapes.

content:
In the Mile High City, the fight is on for the future of the middle tier.

A brewer threw the first punch — or at least, the first one in the public eye. In early September, Constellation Brands, the country’s third-largest macrobrewer, told its wholesaler in Denver, Coors Distributing Company (CDC), that it was terminating its arrangement within 30 days. Mark Anthony Group, which ranks fourth behind the Modelo maker in off-premise sales, followed suit less than two weeks later. Sierra Nevada Brewing Company, the country’s second-largest craft brewer by Brewers Association-defined production volume, made its own move for the exit earlier this month.

The dominoes fell so fast, and from a westward territory, that your humble Hop Take columnist heard echoes of Republic National Distributing Company’s collapse in California, which started with rapid-fire departures by major liquor suppliers at the top of 2025, and ended with the mega-distributor’s de facto demise earlier this year. Was it a social contagion? Blood in the water? Something else?

It’s in vogue for beverage-alcohol industry c-suiters to blame abstractions like “headwinds,” and “Zoomers” whenever trouble arises. But my reporting on RNDC’s California cataclysm indicated bad business decisions, institutional arrogance, and infrastructural rot had pushed the firm to the brink right as the hangover in post-Covid booze sales began to bite. There are always causes, and some are always more proximate than others.

So what’s the casus belli for Colorado’s middle-tier trench war? The militants aren’t saying much.

“We’re exploring all legal and commercial options,” CDC tells Hop Take via email. “None of the parties provided any reason for their termination and doing so without cause is a direct violation of the Colorado beer franchise law.” The firm, a wholly owned distributorship of Molson Coors Brewing Beverage Co., has already asked Denver’s district court to enjoin Constellation and Mark Anthony from exiting; it is “evaluat[ing] next steps with Sierra Nevada.”

“We have concluded our partnership with Coors Distributing Company and remain grateful for their partnership over the years,” says Ellie Preslar, Sierra Nevada’s chief growth officer, in an emailed statement. “Though this was a difficult decision, it is necessary for both the long-term and short-term needs of our business.”

A spokesperson for Constellation declined to comment, citing the litigation. Mark Anthony did not respond.

What gives? I doubt it’s frustration over facilities. After all, in a bit of incredibly unfortunate timing, CDC just cut the ribbon on a new state-of-the-art, 70,000 square-foot warehouse at the end of August, less than two weeks before Constellation’s pink slip. If you work at or with CDC, and know more, please get in touch by emailing dave@dinfontay.com or texting dinfontay.11 on Signal. (You can remain anonymous in my coverage.) But in the meantime, tune your ear to another echo of RNDC’s retreat from the Golden State, because suppliers aren’t just leaving CDC — they’re heading to Reyes Beverage Group. Or at least, trying to.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but often rhymes, and it’s rhyming in the Rockies right now. “How much RNDC blood is on Reyes’s hands in California?” I asked in a column the week I broke the news that the now-defunct distributor was exiting the market last year. “Maybe more than you think.” I was never able to verify whether RBG was in talks to acquire RNDC CA before its exit, as some sources had claimed. But there’s no doubt the mighty beer-turned-”total beverage” distributor’s fierce, many-fronted competition in California hastened RNDC’s failure there. Most of the suppliers who fled pre-collapse, fled to RBG.

A few states east and 18 months later, Mark Anthony and Sierra Nevada have signaled their aims to move their CDC volume to RBG. Constellation has been playing coy, but it’s almost unfathomable that it would move to another house. In a remarkable turn of industry fate, RBG acquired its Colorado operation just this year from, you guessed it: RNDC. Its entry into the state, along with Southern Glazer’s Wine & Spirits’ acquisition of Eagle Rock Distributing Co. earlier this year, has shifted the middle-tier calculus there. Now, CDC is facing subtraction.

(Laurel Slick, RBG’s vice-president of corporate affairs, provided statements to Hop Take welcoming Mark Anthony and Sierra Nevada to the fold.)

But. But! While CDC execs may be uttering f-words privately, they’re uttering another f-word publicly: franchise. The history of franchise law is long, winding, and deathly boring, but the upshot is that beer distributors are nearly unique in the protections afforded to them by most states’ laws. The most crucial of these is the so-called “just cause” provision, which requires brewers to cite a legally defensible breach of their agreement with the house they’re trying to terminate. This provision is written into most states’ codes because wholesalers marched on statehouses to make it so in the ‘60s, ‘70s, and ‘80s. Critics argue it harms competition by making it difficult for good brewers to bail on bad distributors; boosters insist it protects competition by making it difficult for bad brewers to strong-arm good distributors. But it’s there.

The protective power of this provision was tested most famously in Florida roughly a quarter-century ago, and distributors came away with the whip hand. In Maris Distributing v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc., a wholesaler fought the brewer tooth and nail for a decade over a termination it believed unjust. The family — the kin of baseball great Roger Maris, who’d been bestowed an A-B house by Gussie Busch after finishing out his Hall of Fame career with the St. Louis Cardinals — won a $120 million settlement in 2005.

As the mantra goes: there are 50 different states, and 50 different three-tier systems. A version of the just-cause clause is on the books in Colorado. But it’s a weird version. It dictates a brewer hoping to terminate a distributor has to cite “alleged noncompliance” and allow the offending firm 60 days to “cure” the infraction. If the distributor doesn’t shape up in that time, then the brewer can ship out. That’s all right at the top of C.R.S. § 44-3-408. But in subsection three, the code appears to contradict itself, noting “the supplier shall have the right to terminate an agreement with a wholesaler at any time by giving the wholesaler at least ninety days’ written notice by certified mail.” To me, a not-lawyer, , the Colorado code appears to say that a brewer must have just cause to terminate a distributor after 60 days, but can terminate for any reason after 90 days.

You will not be shocked to learn that this is not how CDC’s actual lawyers read the text. “Under Constellation’s novel interpretation of Colorado law, its termination will become final after 90 days,” the firm’s legal team wrote in a September 25 filing. “In the interim, there is a likelihood that CDC will face cascading terminations from its other suppliers.”

For a trade that has long grasped the power of a united political bloc, CDC’s existential fight is cause for alarm. At the National Beer Wholesalers Association’s (NBWA) annual conference in Orlando in mid-October, president and chief executive Craig Purser sounded the klaxons. “The efforts to weaken the three-tier system are going to keep coming, and that’s why we need you to double down on your support and participation in NBWA and your state’s association,” he said, per a dispatch from Brewbound.

Whether the suppliers’ assessments of Colorado’s code are innovative, or illegal, is a matter for the judicial system. But in the meantime, if you’re wondering who the hell would write a statute like that, well, the independent beverage-alcohol bar (ahem) is too. Colorado’s franchise law is “really badly written,” Drew Jaglom of Tannenbaum Helpern Syracuse & Hirschtritt LLP told a presumably sympathetic crowd at the NBWA confab, Brewbound reported.

“What good is a statutory right to cure a breach if a supplier can bypass it simply by waiting another thirty days?” asks Ashley Brandt, the Tucker Ellis LLP attorney behind the prolific trade blotter Libation Law Blog, in a post about the CDC brew-haha. “A supplier that cannot establish a breach—or knows the distributor will fix it—could simply choose the ninety-day route. What happens during those additional thirty days that makes a performing distributor’s continued contractual compliance irrelevant?”

It’s a good question. For CDC, it may wind up being the question. And with the pendulum of power lately swinging back towards big suppliers, you can bet the rest of the middle tier will be hanging on the answer.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Well, Halloween is right around the corner, so it’s a good thing your costume is already covered. What’s that? You’re not wearing the Adult Wedgehead Jumpsuit Costume ($69.99)? The totally epic apparel that corresponds to Shock Top’s Candy Corn Wheat Ale, a new and not-at-all-depressing collaboration between Tilray Brands and retail Grim Reaper Spirit Halloween? Huh. I mean… why not?

📈 Ups…

Stone Brewing co-founders Greg Koch and Steve Wagner are taking over the firm’s recently closed World Bistro & Gardens in Escondido… First-wave craft-brewing pioneer Deschutes will take a crack at the booming “hard sports drink” space with a malt-based offering, Firelyte… Sapporo USA says it has a path to double last year’s volume by the end of 2027… The absolute rubes who bought Ultra Right 100% Woke-Free American Beer back in 2023 still haven’t received it, and Georgia’s attorney general is now investigating, lol… Twin Cities icon Summit Brewing found a new lender to take over its about-to-be-foreclosed-upon loans…

📉 …and downs

Pioneering craft-brewing supplier Admiral Malting announced plans to shutter… Mega-brewers Constellation Brands and Mark Anthony Group are jumping into the “hard sports drink” segment, too — with vodka-based offerings… Centi-billionaire and known freak (but I repeat myself) Mark Zuckerberg finally figured out how to make Guinness look uncool…

Snapping an Instagrammable pic of the aesthetically arranged half shells is one thing — but getting the exact flavor and texture that you want is another. Depending on the variety and location of origin, oysters bring a wide range of flavors. Before diving into the menu, it can be helpful to decide whether you want creamy, almost sweet oysters or briny ones that taste like a gulp of fresh salt water. Beyond flavor, you should also determine if your preferred texture is meaty and hefty or lean and easy to swallow.

To help make your oyster-ordering experience a bit easier, VinePair tapped Ben Crispin, general manager at Maison Premiere, one of Brooklyn’s most celebrated raw bars, to describe the flavors and textures of 15 different varieties. With his help, we charted the oysters across two scales: briny to creamy and lean to meaty.

content:
Working in the service industry, one of the biggest parts of the job is to meet the expectations and wishes of guests. In restaurants, hosts and servers are the business’ first point of contact with the patrons. They are tasked with making sure specific needs are met, such as flagging any allergens or grabbing extra utensils. Likewise, chefs also frequently bend to the whims of their customers, whether that be cooking a burger to a certain temperature or removing raw onions from a side salad.

Most customer modifications are welcome and reasonable, and are a normal part of working in kitchens. But occasionally, a request will come through the kitchen that’s just outright bizarre. That’s why we asked 10 chefs from around the country to name the weirdest demands they’ve ever seen on an order ticket.

From marshmallow fluff dolloped onto a steak to a “vegan” egg white omelet, these are the craziest dish modifications that guests have asked for, according to chefs.

The weirdest dish mods chefs have ever received:

  • Marshmallow fluff on everything
  • Deep-fried steaks
  • Prime rib sandwich mixed into farmhouse salad
  • Ground ribeye burger served with packaging labels
  • No ginger, garlic, onion, or cilantro
  • Steak cooked half-rare and half-well done
  • Well-done steak tartare
  • Non-fried fried oyster mushroom sandwich
  • Vegan egg white omelet
  • Well-done tuna tartare
  • Caesar salad without the lettuce
  • Exactly seven French fries
  • Hamburger that isn’t on the menu

“Early on, a family brought their own marshmallow fluff and asked us to put it on everything their kids ate, including the steak, fries, and salad. We did it, and it was the most disgusting thing I’ve ever seen. We’ve also had guests ask us to cook their steak in the deep fryer because they only eat things that are deep-fried.” —Mark Bucher, co-owner, Medium Rare, New York City

“A few months after opening Millstone, we had a guest request one of the more unusual modifications I’ve seen: combining our smoked prime rib sandwich with our farmhouse salad. They wanted everything — the warm, thinly-shaved smoked ribeye, caramelized onions, melted provolone, mixed field greens, seasonal vegetables, and crumbled goat cheese — all chopped up and tossed together with our horseradish aioli as the dressing. Essentially, they turned two completely different dishes into one very unconventional steak salad. Nearly a year into service, it’s still one of the most memorable requests we’ve received.” —Tyler Murray, chef, Millstone, Lexington, Ky.

“One of the strangest modification requests I’ve had was a guest who asked us to grind a ribeye steak to make his burger, replace the fries with a salad, and bring out the original packaging for every ingredient so he could personally verify the allergens. He told us he had both a citrus allergy and a ‘greens allergy,’ and said that the price should be reduced because he wasn’t getting the standard sides. After about 40 minutes of us trying every possible way to accommodate him, he took off his shoes and socks and put them on the empty chair next to him. When we finally explained that there were simply some requests we couldn’t safely or reasonably fulfill, he responded, ‘So the chef is refusing to make my meal?’” —Clinton Snowling, vice president of culinary operations, Parched Hospitality Group, NYC and West Palm Beach, Fla.

“Cilantro, ginger, garlic, and onion are part of every Indian and South Asian dish, especially on Drāvida’s menu. One of the craziest modifications was when a guest walked in and said they cannot eat ginger, garlic, onion, nor cilantro. We still made it happen: We made them two amazing dishes from scratch using spices and herbs that would make the sauces flavorful. Instead of using onions, we used leeks and they enjoyed it.” —Aarthi Sampath, chef and founder, Drāvida, NYC

“I have worked in a variety of styles of kitchens, so I’ve seen some weird stuff. But I think the modification that takes the cake was when someone asked for a flat iron steak cooked half-rare and half-well done. Then, the server came back to the kitchen and said the guest was adamant about it ‘not being cut in half,’ which I still think about it to this day. Thankfully, the guest was eventually receptive to ordering another dish.” —Mikey Miller, chef, Field Note at The Ashbrook Hotel, Frankfort, Ky.

“One of the strangest requests I’ve ever received was for a well-done steak tartare. Considering the dish is traditionally served raw, it definitely caught me and our team off guard. At that point, you’re not really ordering steak tartare anymore, but we did our best to capture the flavors of the dish.” —Adam Plitt, executive chef, Delmonico’s Hospitality Group, NYC

“The weirdest dish modification I’ve ever gotten was when a guest didn’t want anything fried, but still wanted a fried oyster mushroom sandwich. So, I had to roast all the ingredients in the oven. It took significantly longer to make, like upwards 30 minutes for a sandwich that otherwise took less than three minutes to get out. The server that was helping the table tried to direct them to items on the menu that didn’t include any fried elements, but they were set on this particular item and then lectured me on the unhealthiness of frying food. Nonetheless, it was very early in my career, and I didn’t know it would have been much easier to say, ‘No.’” —Haley Duren, executive chef, Long Count, NYC

“We were asked to cook a shared ribeye half-medium rare and half-well done because the couple liked different temperatures. We’ve also gotten ‘medium rare, but closer to rare’ and, my personal favorite, ‘medium rare, but cooked through with no pink.’ Someone also once asked for an egg white omelet with no yolk or cheese because they were vegan. We’ve also had requests for an omelet with no eggs, just mushrooms and spinach.” —Barry Tonks, culinary director, IGC Hospitality, NYC and Orlando, Fla.

“One of the most unusual requests I’ve received was for a tuna tartare, but well done. It caught me off guard because raw tuna is what defines the dish. content:
On Friday, a federal judge dismissed a class action lawsuit against Costco and its private label Kirkland Signature that alleged the “100% de agave” claims on its tequila bottles were fraudulent and misleading. The consumer rights firm Hagens Berman filed the case with the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington at Seattle in November last year after amassing 14 plaintiffs to join the class suit.

The suit claimed Costco knowingly sold tequila with “significant presence of non-agave sugars,” despite labeling its products — including Kirkland Blanco Tequila, Reposado Tequila, Añejo Tequila, Añejo Cristalino Tequila and Extra Tequila Añejo — as “100% de agave” and as “100% agave azul.” The plaintiffs cited results from Site-Specific Natural Isotope Fractionation-Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (SNIF-NMR) testing, a method commonly used by government bodies and other regulatory agencies to compliance-check food and beverage products.

The plaintiffs asserted that Costco’s claims misled consumers, and that they would have steered away from Kirkland’s tequila or paid significantly less had they known it was not made entirely of pure agave. The case also alleged Costco knowingly acquired a false “100% de agave” certification that allowed it to sell its tequilas, which range from $18.69 to $48.99, at high prices in the U.S.

The warehouse grocery chain defended its labels by citing product tests conducted in Mexico, which turned out different results than the plaintiffs’ SNIF-NMR. It also pointed to former cases with similar allegations against, in which a U.S. judge ruled the SNIF-NMR as insufficient evidence to debunk the “100% de agave” label.

Costco is not the only tequila vendor to be thrown under question for its pure agave claims. Last month, a New York judge tossed a similar case against Diageo’s Casamigos and Don Julio brands over insufficient testing. Allegations against Kendall Jenner’s 818 Tequila’s “100% agave” labels have also led to a class action lawsuit, which the company has motioned to dismiss multiple times to no avail.

title: Art and Wine Have a Long History. But Does Art Sell Wine?
summary:
